title: Choosing the right denominator for refund rate
prompt: Support wants a "refund rate" for last quarter. Which denominator is correct?
grain: One rate, computed from a ratio of two counts.

options.label: All orders placed in the quarter, including cancelled ones
Completed orders placed in the quarter
All refund requests submitted in the quarter

explanation: Refund rate should measure refunds as a share of orders that could plausibly be refunded — completed orders. Including cancelled orders inflates the denominator with orders that were never fulfilled in the first place, and using refund requests as the denominator conflates the numerator's own population with itself.

title: Population for a late payment rate
prompt: Risk wants a "late payment rate" across the loan book. Which population is correct for the denominator?
population: Payments due in the reporting period.
grain: One rate, computed from a ratio of two counts.

options.label: All payments due in the period, across every loan status
Payments due in the period for loans that are currently active (not closed or defaulted)
Only the payments that were actually late in the period

explanation: Closed and defaulted loans shouldn't count toward a rate meant to flag emerging risk on the current book, and using only the late payments as the denominator would make the rate always equal 100%.

title: What does a row represent after aggregating MRR by account?
prompt: Finance wants monthly recurring revenue by account. Subscriptions start at one row per subscription change. After building what finance asked for, what does one row of the result represent?
grain: Ends at one row per account per month.

options.label: One account, across its entire lifetime

explanation: "Monthly" recurring revenue by account means the result needs a row per account per month, not per raw change event and not collapsed across all months into one row per account.

title: Order the pipeline: on-time rate by loan origination cohort
prompt: You need on-time payment rate grouped by the month each loan originated. Put these steps in the order they need to happen.
population: Payments due in the reporting window, for loans with a known origination month.
grain: Ends at one row per origination cohort (month).

steps.label: Filter payments to those due in the reporting window
Join payments to loans to get each loan's origination month (the cohort)
Aggregate to one row per origination cohort: count on-time and total payments
Calculate the rate: on-time payments divided by total payments

explanation: The cohort (origination month) only exists on the loans table, so it has to be joined in before you can group by it. Grouping has to happen before dividing two aggregated counts — you can't calculate a per-cohort rate from ungrouped rows.

title: Order the pipeline: repeat customers by month
prompt: Marketing wants, for each month, how many customers placed more than one completed order that month. Put these blocks in the order they need to run.
grain: Ends at one row per month.

steps.label: Aggregate to one row per customer per month, counting orders
Filter those rows to where the order count is greater than 1
Count the distinct customers left, per month

explanation: You can't filter on "order count per customer per month" until that count exists, which means aggregating first. Filtering the aggregated rows down to repeat customers has to happen before the final count, or the count would include everyone.

title: Order the pipeline: expansion MRR month over month
prompt: Finance wants expansion MRR: for accounts whose MRR increased from the prior month, the sum of that increase, by month. Put these blocks in the order they need to run.
grain: Ends at one row per month.

steps.label: Aggregate subscriptions to one row per account per month (MRR)
Apply LAG to get each account's MRR in the prior month
Filter to rows where MRR increased versus the prior month
Sum the positive deltas by month

explanation: LAG needs one row per account per month to look back a month, so aggregation has to happen first. Filtering to increases only makes sense once the delta (current vs. prior) exists, and summing by month comes last.

title: Investigate: checkout conversion dropped last week
prompt: Checkout conversion dropped 15% last week. You have 10 credits to spend investigating before recommending a root cause — you don't need to buy every investigation.
population: Checkout sessions from the last two weeks.

investigations.label: Check the payment gateway error rate
investigations.revealText: Payment gateway error rate roughly doubled starting the same day the drop began.

investigations.label: Check traffic source mix
investigations.revealText: Traffic source mix is unchanged week over week.

investigations.label: Check for pricing or promo changes
investigations.revealText: No pricing or promo changes were made that week.

investigations.label: Check for a recent checkout UI deploy
investigations.revealText: No checkout UI deploy happened that week.

recommendationOptions.label: Escalate to the payments team — a gateway issue is likely causing failed checkouts
Escalate to marketing — traffic quality likely dropped
Escalate to pricing — a promo change likely hurt conversion

explanation: The payment gateway error rate spike lines up exactly with when the drop started, and nothing else changed (traffic mix, pricing, UI) — that's the cheapest investigation that already explains the drop on its own.

title: GROUP BY vs. window function for a running loan balance
prompt: You need each loan's running total of disbursed amount over time, without collapsing its individual disbursement rows. Which approach is correct?
grain: Keeps one row per disbursement, plus a running total column.

options.label: GROUP BY loan_id, ORDER BY disbursed_at
SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY loan_id ORDER BY disbursed_at)
A subquery that re-runs SUM(amount) for each row with no partitioning

explanation: GROUP BY collapses rows into one per group, which loses the individual disbursement rows you need to keep. A window function with PARTITION BY/ORDER BY keeps every row while adding the running total; the unpartitioned subquery would sum across every loan instead of just the current one.
